title: Aslana, Queering the King
author: Annie Crawford
summary: Crawford uses the announcement that Meryl Streep will voice Aslan in Greta Gerwig's adaptation of The Magician's Nephew to make a case about how symbols carry meaning. Her premise, borrowed from Michael Ward's essay on onions and roses, is that created things have intrinsic qualities we cannot assign at will, and that Lewis could build a re-enchanted Narnia because his imagination was sacramental in exactly this way. She grants that adaptation always requires change, and even concedes that swapping a character's gender can leave a story's heart intact. The hinge of the argument is that Aslan is not one character among others but the figure who stands for Christ inside Lewis's cosmos, so altering his sex inverts the polarity of creator and creation on which the whole imaginary world rests. Crawford supports this with Lewis's own writing on gender and his essay opposing the feminization of God, then with his treatment of kingliness in Planet Narnia and That Hideous Strength. She concludes that queenliness has its own glory but cannot substitute for kingliness, and that no Narnia film would be preferable to this one.
points: Grounds the objection in a theory of intrinsic meaning drawn from Michael Ward, arguing that objects in a story carry given significance rather than assigned significance.
Distinguishes between adaptive changes that preserve a story's essential theme and changes that destroy its allusive structure, using the apple, the pomegranate and the onion as test cases.
Concedes that recasting Lucy or Susan as male would be survivable, which isolates Aslan's significance as the actual point of dispute.
Marshals Lewis's own claim that gender is more fundamental than sex, and his essay on priestesses, to argue that feminizing the creator amounts to a different religion.
Reads kingliness as a governing theme across Planet Narnia and That Hideous Strength, so that a Narnia without a king loses the object of worship the books were written to evoke.
quotes: We love our favorite stories because they provide a frame through which we can understand who we are and the world we live in.
Lewis could write such a world because his imagination was deeply sacramental. He understood that created things like wardrobes, lamp posts, and lions are formed with intrinsic meaning.

Any filmmaker will necessarily adapt various aspects of a novel and change certain details; the transposition from the written word to the visually dominant, time-bound media of film makes this inevitable.

But to change the gender of The Lion, of The King, of the Incarnate Son of the Emperor Across the Sea who symbolically represents the deity of Christ within Lewis’s imaginary world is to completely alter the structure and meaning of Lewis’s sacramental cosmos.
The fruitful duality of male and female are symbolic manifestations of the spiritual duality between heaven and earth, creator and creation, Christ and his church.

A world ruled by Aslana is a world quite different in character from Narnia. A story in which the children bow before the Lioness is a story quite different in character than the Chronicles of Narnia.
Queenliness has its own great glories, as Lewis explores in the Edenic world of Perelandra, but it is not the same glory as kingliness
Indeed. And it would be better to have no Narnia films than one that comes with this horrible queering of the King.
